newsitem.title: UK: British court quashes Forsyth Polly Peck conviction.
newsitem.headline: British court quashes Forsyth Polly Peck conviction.

text.p: Elizabeth Forsyth, former aide to Polly Peck head Asil Nadir, had her conviction for handling stolen goods overturned on Monday by a London appeal court.

Lord Justice Beldam, one of three judges who heard Forsyth's appeal, ruled her conviction was unsafe and her appeal should be allowed. In January the court overturned Forsyth's five-year jail sentence, of which she had served 10 months.

Beldam said Sir Richard Tucker, the judge at Forsyth's trial, had misdirected the jury during his summing-up of the case. She was found guilty last April of dishonestly handling 400,000 pounds ($640,000).
Forsyth, who walked out of the court linking arms with her 90-year-old mother, said she was "very happy" to have cleared her name.
But she said she wanted it made clear that her conviction had been quashed not on technical grounds but because of the merits of the defence.

"At two vital stages he (the trial judge) virtually directed the jury to convict. I have no doubt that I would have been acquitted by the jury had the judge...not summed up so improperly against me," she said after the ruling was given.

Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the case against 60-year-old Forsyth, said the Court of Appeal's ruling "emphasises the difficuly for judges in giving directions to juries in fraud trials".
But the organisation said the ruling did not affect its case against Nadir himself.

Forsyth said she was pleased the court had criticised the SFO for what she called its "strange" decision to prosecute her, adding that she believed the judges thought it had been "a scapegoat prosecution".

She was chairman of South Audley Management, a firm set up by Nadir to deal with his wealthy faimily businesses before his fruit-to-electronics group Polly Peck empire collapsed in 1990 under the weight of huge debts.

Nadir fled Britain for his native northern Cyprus in 1993, skipping bail of 3.5 million pounds. The outcome of Forsyth's appeal was seen as an indicator of whether Nadir would attempt to have theft and false accounting charges against him dropped, paving the way for his return to Britain.

Peter Krivinskas, who represents both Forsyth and Nadir, said he thought Nadir would shortly instruct him to begin an "abuse of process application", although Nadir would not come back before a decision on this was given.

But the SFO, which has been widely criticised for its failure to secure convictions in several high-profile cases, said of Nadir, "He remains a fugitive from justice and a warrant for his arrest is outstanding."

Forsyth said she would take legal advice on how to secure "appropriate compensation" for what she described as a "miscarriage of justice" if she was not offered compensation for wrongful imprisonment.
In a statement she accused the SFO of having attempted to ruin her life, but later said she bore no grudges and declined to comment on the level of compensation she was seeking.
Compensation is usually decided by Britain's interior ministry the Home Office, not by the SFO.
Forsyth's lawyer, while happy with the result of the appeal, told Reuters the case "now demands a full public inquiry into the whole circumstances surrounding Polly Peck".
He added that the ruling vindicated Nadir's view that he would not have got a fair trial.
